vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is a 37-year-old financial analyst who carries himself with the careful precision of someone who has learned, at great cost, that the world can turn without warning. He sits in the consulting room with his back to the wall and his eyes near the door - a habit he barely notices anymore, the way you stop noticing a scar.

Three years ago, Marcus was traveling in a politically unstable region for work, conducting due diligence on a prospective infrastructure investment. He was taken from his hotel room in the early hours of the morning by armed men whose faces he never fully saw. What followed was eleven days of captivity in a series of dark, confined spaces - a van, a basement, a room he estimates was no larger than a bathroom. He was blindfolded for much of it, fed irregularly, and subjected to prolonged periods of silence broken by sudden, unpredictable interrogations. He was not physically tortured, a fact he mentions with something like guilt, as though it disqualifies him from feeling the way he does. He was, however, made to believe on at least two occasions that he was about to be killed. He was eventually released following negotiations he was never fully briefed on, flown home, and given a week of medical clearance before his employer expected him back at his desk.

He returned to his desk. He returned to his marriage, too, though not for long.

In the months that followed, Marcus found that the spreadsheets and models that had once felt like a second language had become incomprehensible noise. He could sit in front of a screen for hours and produce nothing - not because he lacked the knowledge, but because concentration had become something that happened to other people. He describes his mind as a room with too many doors, each one opening onto the basement, the blindfold, the voice telling him to stay quiet. His sleep, when it comes, delivers him back there reliably. He wakes at three or four in the morning with his heart already running, certain for several seconds that the darkness around him is that darkness.

His wife, Elena, tried to reach him. He knows this now in a way he couldn't then. At the time, her concern felt like surveillance, her questions like interrogations. He became withdrawn and then, when withdrawal wasn't enough, he became sharp with her in ways he is still ashamed of. She left fourteen months after the kidnapping. He tells this part of the story flatly, the way you describe weather.

He lives alone now in a flat he chose for its ground-floor location - he cannot reliably use lifts - and its proximity to two different exit routes from the building. He works remotely when his employer allows it, which is most of the time. On days when he must go into the office, he plans his route, his seat, his exits. He avoids the underground. He avoids crowded restaurants, hotel lobbies, anywhere that smells like industrial cleaning fluid, which takes him back to the van with a specificity that still shocks him.

He doesn't talk about what happened, not really. He told the story once to a colleague who asked too directly at a work drinks event, and watched the man's face cycle through fascination and discomfort and then settle on a kind of impressed distance, as though Marcus had become a different category of person. He hasn't told it since.

What Marcus talks about instead, when he talks at all, is the feeling of being permanently slightly outside of things - watching his own life the way you watch a market you no longer have a position in. He is intelligent enough to know something has shifted in him and honest enough to say he doesn't know how to shift it back. He comes to sessions on time, every time, and he sits with his back to the wall, and he begins, carefully, to speak.
